entities.EARTH: planet Earth seen from space, accurate continents and oceans, white swirling cloud systems, thin glowing blue atmospheric limb, black space background with faint stars
entities.MOON: Earth's Moon with its accurate near-side pattern of dark grey maria and bright highlands, realistic apparent size, no exaggeration
entities.CITY: an unnamed modern coastal city skyline at night with warm sodium and white LED lights, no recognizable landmarks
entities.COAST: a rocky temperate coastline with a wide tidal flat, wet sand reflecting the sky, kelp-covered boulders
entities.REEF: an Indo-Pacific Acropora coral reef, branching and table corals
entities.NIGHT_SKY: a natural dark night sky full of stars with the Milky Way band, faint green airglow near the horizon

cuts.narration: Tonight, at nine forty-one p.m., the Moon is gone. No explosion. No flash. One moment it hangs over the city. The next, there is only black sky.
cuts.purpose: Hook: the Moon disappears over a city
cuts.subject: full Moon above a city skyline that suddenly vanishes
cuts.prompt: Slow push-in from a rooftop toward a bright full MOON hanging above CITY at night; after two seconds the Moon silently vanishes with no explosion and no flash, leaving only black starry sky; city lights keep glowing; calm, eerie, no camera shake
cuts.science_notes: Dramatization. The vanishing must be silent and instant — no explosion (matches the premise).

cuts.narration: So what breaks first? The answer is stranger than the movies. Because the most dangerous change is the slowest one.
cuts.subject: people on a rooftop looking up at an empty night sky
cuts.camera_angle: medium wide, from behind the people
cuts.lighting: city glow from below, dark sky above
cuts.prompt: Three people seen from behind standing on a CITY rooftop at night, looking up at an empty dark sky with no moon, city glow lighting their silhouettes from below, sense of unease

cuts.narration: First, the rules. Nothing in physics lets a whole world simply vanish. Mass and energy don't just disappear. So this is a thought experiment.
cuts.purpose: State that this is a thought experiment
cuts.subject: title card

params.title: A THOUGHT EXPERIMENT
params.subtitle: Physically impossible — and that's the point

cuts.narration: We delete the Moon instantly and completely. Its light, its gravity, everything. Then we follow the consequences, from the first second to the next hundred million years.
cuts.purpose: Show the time ladder the video follows
cuts.subject: timeline

cuts.narration: And we'll keep score honestly: what scientists have measured, what physics lets us infer, and where the experts still disagree.
cuts.subject: three labels

cuts.narration: Second zero. In a disaster movie, Earth would be flung out of its orbit. That doesn't happen.
cuts.subject: Earth alone in space
cuts.camera_angle: wide, Earth small in frame, Sun glare at edge
cuts.prompt: EARTH alone in the blackness of space, small in the frame, harsh sunlight from the left edge of frame, vast emptiness, sense of scale, no moon visible

cuts.narration: Earth and the Moon actually circle a shared balance point. Because Earth is about eighty-one times heavier, that point sits inside our planet, roughly four thousand seven hundred kilometers from the center.
cuts.subject: barycenter inside Earth
cuts.onscreen_text: Balance point: ~4,700 km from Earth's center

cuts.narration: Every month, Earth makes a small loop around it, at about twelve meters per second. Our speed around the Sun is nearly thirty kilometers per second.
cuts.subject: bar comparison
cuts.science_notes: C03, C04 (12 m/s is a calculation: 2π×4,671 km / 27.32 d). Log scale is labelled.

cuts.narration: Delete the Moon, and that little loop simply straightens out. Our path around the Sun barely changes. Nobody would feel a thing.
cuts.subject: Earth and the Sun
cuts.prompt: Wide view of EARTH in space with the Sun as a brilliant star far to the right, calm and serene, thin crescent of daylight on the planet, peaceful mood

cuts.narration: What people would notice first is the dark.
cuts.subject: lone figure in a desert under a moonless sky
cuts.prompt: A lone person standing in a vast desert at night under a moonless NIGHT_SKY, only starlight illuminating the sand dunes faintly, very dark, Milky Way overhead

cuts.narration: A full Moon on a clear night lights the ground with about a quarter of a lux. Without it, a natural sky offers starlight and faint airglow, around a hundredth of that.
cuts.subject: log scale of illuminance

cuts.narration: In cities, streetlights would hide the change. But in the deserts, the oceans and the forests, every night would become a new-moon night. Forever.
cuts.subject: dark forest by a lake under stars, distant city glow
cuts.lighting: starlight, faint orange skyglow on the horizon
cuts.prompt: A dark pine forest beside a still lake at night under a moonless NIGHT_SKY, stars reflected in the water, a faint orange glow of a distant city on the horizon

cuts.narration: Some animals are tuned to that light. Dung beetles in Africa steer by polarized moonlight, and on moonless nights they hold their course by the glow of the Milky Way.
cuts.purpose: Animals that navigate by night light
cuts.subject: dung beetle rolling a ball
cuts.prompt: Macro ground-level photo of a dung beetle rolling a dung ball across dry savanna soil at night, the Milky Way band glowing in the sky behind, dim silvery starlight, shallow depth of field
cuts.science_notes: C08: Scarabaeus satyrus-type nocturnal beetle; keep it realistic.

cuts.narration: On coral reefs, many species spawn together, timed to the lunar cycle. A light-sensitive gene in these corals is most active under full-moon light.
cuts.purpose: Coral spawning tied to the Moon
cuts.subject: corals releasing egg bundles
cuts.prompt: Underwater night photo of REEF during mass spawning, branching corals releasing countless small pink and orange egg-sperm bundles that drift upward like an inverted snowfall, soft blue light filtering from the surface

cuts.narration: Without that clock, spawning could drift out of sync, and eggs released on different nights may never meet. How badly this would play out is still an open question.
cuts.subject: sparse eggs in dark water
cuts.prompt: Very dark underwater night scene over REEF, only a few scattered coral egg bundles drifting alone in the black-blue water, lonely and quiet mood

cuts.narration: Hour six. Along the coast, the tide comes in, and stops short.
cuts.subject: tide coming in and stopping short
cuts.camera_angle: low wide shot over the tidal flat
cuts.prompt: Low wide shot over COAST tidal flat in overcast daylight; shallow waves slide in over the wet sand, then slow and stop well short of the old high-water line marked by dark seaweed on the rocks; calm, quiet, no people
cuts.science_notes: C12 — dramatized illustration of smaller tides.

cuts.narration: The Moon raises most of our tides. The Sun raises tides too, but its tidal pull is only about forty-six percent of the Moon's.
cuts.subject: bars Moon vs Sun

cuts.narration: So the tides don't vanish. They shrink, to roughly a third of their typical size. And they follow the Sun's rhythm, with high water at nearly the same time every day.
cuts.subject: bars
cuts.science_notes: C12: 0.46/1.46 ≈ 0.32; global rule of thumb, local tides vary.

cuts.narration: There is no giant wave either. The ocean's tidal bulge is subtle, well under a meter in open water. So the sea would settle over hours, like an ordinary falling tide.
cuts.subject: open ocean at dusk
cuts.prompt: Calm open ocean at dusk seen from low above the water, gentle long swell, soft pastel sky, peaceful, endless horizon

cuts.narration: Spring tides and neap tides end, too. They come from the Sun and Moon lining up, and now there is nothing to line up with.
cuts.subject: alignment diagram

cuts.narration: That matters. Tides flush estuaries and feed the strip of shore that is underwater half the day and dry the other half. With weaker tides, that strip narrows, and the life adapted to it loses ground.
cuts.subject: rock pool with starfish and anemones
cuts.prompt: Top-down close photo of an intertidal rock pool on COAST at low tide, orange starfish, green anemones, mussels and barnacles, clear water, bright overcast light

cuts.narration: Year one. There will never be another total solar eclipse. Only the Moon could cover the Sun.
cuts.subject: total solar eclipse over mountains
cuts.prompt: Total solar eclipse above a mountain landscape, the black disk of the MOON surrounded by the Sun's white glowing corona, 360-degree twilight glow on the horizon, people silhouetted on a ridge

cuts.narration: Something quieter changes, too. Today, tidal friction acts like a brake on Earth's spin. It adds roughly two milliseconds to the day every century, and pushes the Moon about three point eight centimeters farther away each year.
cuts.subject: two number cards

cuts.narration: Without the Moon, most of that brake is released. You would never notice it in a lifetime. But over hundreds of millions of years, Earth's days would stay shorter than they otherwise would have.
cuts.subject: sunrise over Earth from orbit
cuts.prompt: Sunrise seen from low orbit over EARTH, the Sun breaking over the curved horizon, the day-night terminator line crossing cloud systems, thin blue atmosphere

cuts.narration: Now, the real danger. And it is slow.
cuts.subject: Earth half in shadow
cuts.prompt: EARTH half in deep shadow and half lit by hard sunlight from the side, ominous and still, the planet slightly tilted in the frame

cuts.narration: Earth spins on a tilted axis, about twenty-three degrees. That tilt is why we have seasons.
cuts.subject: tilted Earth

params.title: Axial tilt ≈ 23.4°
params.caption: The tilt is why we have seasons

cuts.narration: Today it only rocks gently, between roughly twenty-two and twenty-four and a half degrees, over tens of thousands of years.
cuts.subject: range bar

cuts.narration: The Moon is a big reason why. Its gravity tugs on Earth's bulging waist, and drives about two-thirds of the slow wobble of our axis, called precession.
cuts.subject: pie chart

cuts.narration: That wobble keeps Earth's spin out of step with the gentle, repeating tugs of the other planets.
cuts.subject: Earth with distant planets
cuts.prompt: Deep-space view of EARTH and the MOON small in the foreground, with Jupiter and Venus as bright points far in the background, quiet cosmic scale, cinematic composition
cuts.science_notes: C23 — artistic; real planets are far smaller in the sky.

cuts.narration: Remove the Moon, and the wobble slows down, and it can fall into rhythm with those tugs. In 1993, Jacques Laskar and his colleagues calculated that a moonless Earth's tilt could wander chaotically, anywhere from near zero to about eighty-five degrees.
cuts.subject: range bar

cuts.narration: Near the top of that range, much of the planet would face months of endless daylight, followed by months of darkness.
cuts.subject: midnight sun over frozen land
cuts.prompt: Midnight sun hanging low over a frozen high-latitude landscape, long shadows on snow and ice, golden light, endless daylight feeling, no people

cuts.narration: But here is the twist. In 2011, a team led by Jack Lissauer ran direct simulations, and found far narrower swings. Roughly ten to twenty degrees, over hundreds of millions of years.
cuts.subject: range bar

params.title: Two studies, two answers
params.footnote: Lissauer band drawn as ±10° around today for illustration

cuts.science_notes: C24. The Lissauer band is illustrative (±10° around 23.4°); the paper reports variation size, not a fixed window.

cuts.narration: Even that is a different world. Today the tilt shifts by about two and a half degrees. A twenty-degree swing would redraw where ice sheets grow, where monsoons fall, and where crops can survive.
cuts.subject: ice sheet edge next to farmland and monsoon clouds
cuts.prompt: Aerial view of a vast ice sheet edge meeting green farmland, towering monsoon storm clouds in the distance, dramatic shafts of light, sense of a changing climate

cuts.narration: And none of it happens fast. These changes unfold over tens of thousands to millions of years. Slow for us. Fast for a planet.
cuts.subject: timeline highlight
cuts.onscreen_text: Tens of thousands → millions of years

cuts.narration: So, what breaks first? Not the orbit. Not the length of the day. First, the dark. Then the tides. And last, slowly, the steady footing of our seasons.
cuts.subject: moonless coastline at night, city lights far away
cuts.prompt: COAST at night under a moonless NIGHT_SKY, small calm waves on the sand, a distant CITY glowing on the far shore, contemplative mood

cuts.narration: In reality, the Moon isn't going anywhere soon. Laser beams bounced off mirrors left by Apollo astronauts show it drifting away by just three point eight centimeters a year.
cuts.subject: observatory laser beam aimed at the Moon
cuts.prompt: A mountain-top astronomical observatory at night firing a thin bright green laser beam toward the MOON high in the sky, telescope dome open, clear starry sky
cuts.science_notes: C18 — lunar laser ranging is real; beam visibility is stylised.

cuts.narration: Our scenario is impossible. But it shows what the Moon really is. A lamp. A clock for the oceans. And a hand on the steering wheel of our seasons.
cuts.subject: Earth and Moon together
cuts.prompt: EARTH and the MOON together in one frame, both lit by warm sunlight from the same side, the Moon smaller and farther away, a quiet portrait of the pair

cuts.narration: Tonight, look up. It is still there, holding everything steady.
cuts.subject: person on a hill watching the Moon rise
cuts.prompt: A person sitting on a grassy hilltop at blue hour, seen from behind, watching a full MOON rise over distant hills and a town, peaceful and warm
